scenes: January eighth, eighteen fifteen.
January 8, 1815.
A sugar field, five miles below New Orleans.
It's just before dawn, and the fog is so thick a man can't see the end of his own musket.
Somewhere out in it, about eight thousand British soldiers are forming up.
Many of them have just beaten Napoleon's armies in Spain.
In front of them is a ditch, a wall of mud, and an army that shouldn't exist.
And the war they are about to fight... is already over.
America and Britain had been at war for two and a half years.
It had not gone well for the Americans.
The summer before, British troops had marched into Washington and burned the White House.
Now they wanted New Orleans.
Whoever held that city held the mouth of the Mississippi, and everything that floated down it.
So they sent a fleet, and an army, and a general named Edward Packinum.
So they sent a fleet, and an army, and a general named Edward Pakenham.
Waiting for him was Andrew Jackson.
Jackson was thin, sick, and too stubborn to lie down.
And he had no real army.
So he built one, out of whatever was in reach.
A few regular soldiers. Sailors and Marines.
Militia from Tennessee and Kentucky, some of them without a gun to their name.
Shopkeepers and lawyers from the city.
Two battalions of free Black men. A company of Choctaw.
And the pirates of Zhawn Lafitte, who knew how to run a cannon.
And the pirates of Jean Lafitte, who knew how to run a cannon.
About five thousand men, who had never fought together.
Jackson picked his ground carefully.
An old canal ran across a plantation, from the river on one side, to a cypress swamp on the other.
Less than a mile wide.
And no way around it.
Behind that ditch, they piled up mud.
Enslaved men did much of the digging.
For two weeks the wall grew, with cannon set along the top.
Then they stood behind it, and waited.
Packinum's plan was a good one.
Pakenham's plan was a good one.
One force would cross the river in the night, take the American guns on the far bank, and turn them on Jackson's line.
Then the main army would cross the field in the dark, fill the ditch with bundles of cane, throw ladders against the wall, and go over.
Almost none of that happened.
The boats got stuck in the mud, and the river force crossed hours late.
And the regiment that was supposed to carry the ladders... marched right past them.
By the time the sky was turning gray, Packinum had a choice.
By the time the sky was turning gray, Pakenham had a choice.
Call it off. Or go anyway.
He fired the rocket.
The British came on through the fog, in perfect lines, drums going.
And then the fog lifted.
They were in the open, on a flat field, in red coats, in front of every gun Jackson had.
The cannon opened first.
Then the rifles.
Then the muskets, rank after rank, one stepping up as the last stepped back to load.
It did not stop.
The men who reached the ditch looked for the ladders.
There were no ladders.
So they stood there.
And they died there.
Packinum rode forward to rally them.
Pakenham rode forward to rally them.
He was hit. Then hit again.
He did not live out the morning.
His second in command went down. Then his third.
One regiment of Highlanders was marched across the field, halted in the open, and given no further order.
So they stood at attention, under the guns... because nobody told them to move.
All across the field, soldiers lay down among the dead, just to stay alive.
The main attack lasted about half an hour.
The British lost more than two thousand men. Killed, wounded, or captured.
The Americans lost seventy one.
The Americans lost 71.
Thirteen of them dead.
13 of them dead.
A Kentucky soldier looked over the wall, and said the field was entirely covered with bodies.
And then, some of them stood up.
Living men, who had lain down in the mud, and now walked in to surrender.
Here is the part nobody on that field knew.
Fifteen days earlier, on Christmas Eve, in a city in Belgium, the two countries had signed a peace.
15 days earlier, on Christmas Eve, in a city in Belgium, the two countries had signed a peace.
The news was on a ship, still crossing the Atlantic.
The treaty still had to be approved.
But its terms were set, and nothing won at New Orleans changed a word of them.
So what did the battle change?
On paper, nothing.
But the country didn't read it that way.
The news of the victory and the news of the peace arrived almost together, and Americans decided they had won the war.
A patchwork army had beaten the best soldiers in the world.
And the man behind that mud wall rode it all the way to the White House.
The last great battle of the war... was fought after the peace was signed.
And it mattered anyway.
